title: Math, randomness and hashing in Fabric Warehouse and SQL analytics endpoint
summary: RAND and CRYPT_GEN_RANDOM are not supported. Build random values from NEWID instead. NEWID, CHECKSUM, BINARY_CHECKSUM, HASHBYTES, GREATEST/LEAST and the bit functions are available. The SQL Server typing rules still apply and still bite silently: integer division truncates, POWER returns the type of its first argument, and ROUND/FLOOR/CEILING keep decimal types. Default varchar is UTF-8, which changes the bytes that HASHBYTES sees.

claims.statement: RAND is not supported in Fabric. Any query that calls RAND(), with or without a seed, fails at compile time.
claims.sql_server: RAND() works. Without a seed it is evaluated once per query, not once per row.
claims.alternative: Use NEWID-based randomness, which is evaluated per row: ABS(CAST(CHECKSUM(NEWID()) AS bigint)) / 2147483648.0 gives a value in [0,1).

claims.statement: The usual RAND replacement is CHECKSUM(NEWID()). Cast it to bigint before ABS. CHECKSUM can return -2147483648, and ABS of that int overflows at run time.
claims.probe_sql: SELECT ABS(CAST(CHECKSUM(NEWID()) AS bigint)) % 100 AS bucket;
claims.sql_server: Same overflow risk with ABS(CHECKSUM(NEWID())) on int.

claims.statement: CRYPT_GEN_RANDOM is not supported, so you cannot generate cryptographic random bytes in T-SQL here.
claims.sql_server: CRYPT_GEN_RANDOM(n) returns n random bytes from the crypto API.
claims.alternative: For non-security uses, CAST(NEWID() AS varbinary(16)) gives 16 random-looking bytes. Generate real secrets outside the warehouse.

claims.statement: NEWID exists and returns uniqueidentifier. It is evaluated per row, so it works for random ordering and sampling (ORDER BY NEWID()).

HASHBYTES exists. The hash depends on the bytes of the input: varchar and nvarchar of the same text give different hashes. Default Fabric varchar collation is UTF-8, so varchar bytes for non-ASCII text differ from a SQL Server code-page varchar. Cast both sides to the same type before comparing hashes across systems. Prefer SHA2_256 or SHA2_512.
claims.sql_server: varchar uses the collation code page (often Windows-1252), so non-ASCII varchar text hashes differently than in Fabric.

claims.statement: CHECKSUM and BINARY_CHECKSUM exist and return int. They collide often, so do not use them as unique keys or for reliable change detection. For string inputs, CHECKSUM follows collation rules and BINARY_CHECKSUM uses raw bytes.
claims.sql_server: Same int result and same collision risk.

claims.statement: int / int is integer division and silently truncates: 7 / 2 returns 3, not 3.5.
claims.alternative: Make one operand decimal: 7 / 2.0, or CAST(7 AS decimal(10,2)) / 2.

claims.statement: POWER returns the type of its first argument. POWER(2, 0.5) returns int 1, and POWER(2, -1) returns 0, both silently wrong.
claims.alternative: Pass a float or decimal first argument: POWER(CAST(2 AS float), 0.5).

claims.statement: SQRT, LOG, LOG10 and EXP return float even for int input, so expect binary floating-point rounding. LOG takes an optional base as the second argument: LOG(8, 2).
claims.alternative: Cast to decimal after the call if you need exact scale.

claims.statement: ROUND keeps the input decimal type. ROUND(748.58, -1) stays numeric(5,2). Rounding that needs an extra digit, such as ROUND(748.58, -4), overflows at run time instead of returning 10000.
claims.sql_server: Same documented behaviour: ROUND(748.58, -4) raises an arithmetic overflow.

claims.statement: FLOOR and CEILING on decimal return a decimal with scale 0, not int. On float they return float. Cast explicitly if you need an integer type.
GREATEST and LEAST exist. They ignore NULL arguments and return NULL only when every argument is NULL. Mixed argument types are promoted by data type precedence.
claims.sql_server: Available from SQL Server 2022 with the same NULL handling. Older code uses CASE or a VALUES subquery with MAX.

claims.statement: The bit functions BIT_COUNT, GET_BIT and SET_BIT exist. BIT_COUNT returns bigint, not int.
claims.probe_sql: SELECT BIT_COUNT(CAST(255 AS int)) AS n;

claims.statement: LEFT_SHIFT and RIGHT_SHIFT exist and return the type of their first argument. Bits shifted past the type width are lost silently, with no overflow error.
claims.alternative: Use a bigint first argument when you need more than 32 bits.
